title: Lab Week 04
text:
What is an API?
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that lets your code talk to a remote server and request data. Instead of downloading a file manually from a website, you send a structured request to a URL and receive structured data back. This is the foundation of reproducible data acquisition: your script is the download step.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Downloading Earthquake Data
We begin with the simplest possible API example. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) publishes a real-time feed of recent earthquakes as GeoJSON. Because geopandas can read GeoJSON directly from a URL, a single line of code is enough to turn this feed into a spatial dataframe.
The USGS earthquake feed at earthquake.usgs.gov returns all magnitude 2.5+ earthquakes from the past seven days.

import geopandas as gpd

# Download data on magnitude 2.5+ quakes from the past week
endpoint_url = (
     "http://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/2.5_week.geojson"
 )
earthquakes = gpd.read_file(endpoint_url)
print(earthquakes.head())

That is the entire script. The key insight is that the USGS server returns a GeoJSON FeatureCollection, which is a format that GeoPandas understands natively. No authentication is required for this feed.






Try it yourself



Run the code above and inspect the resulting dataframe. What columns are available? Try plotting the earthquakes on a world map with earthquakes.plot(). You can also colour the points by magnitude: earthquakes.plot(column="mag", cmap="OrRd", legend=True).

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Understanding the Pattern
Even though this example is short, it demonstrates the core API pattern that we will use throughout this lab:







Step
What happens




1. Construct a URL
The URL encodes what you want (earthquake data, magnitude 2.5+, past week)


2. Send a request
gpd.read_file() sends an HTTP GET request to the server


3. Parse the response
The GeoJSON response is automatically converted to a GeoDataFrame



In Parts 2 and 3, we will see how to add query parameters, authentication, and more complex workflows, but the fundamental pattern remains the same.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 1: Query the API
Unlike the USGS feed, the CARTO API takes query parameters. We pass a SQL query (q), the output format (format), and optionally which fields to skip.

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import requests
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

pd.options.display.max_columns = 999

# The API endpoint
carto_api_endpoint = "https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql"

# The query parameters
params = {
    "q": "SELECT * FROM shootings",
    "format": "geojson",
    "skipfields": "cartodb_id",
}

response = requests.get(carto_api_endpoint, params=params)
response







SQL via API



The CARTO SQL API is powerful because it lets you run arbitrary SQL queries on the server side. This means you can filter and aggregate data before downloading it, reducing both bandwidth and processing time on your local machine.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 2: Parse the Response
The response is a GeoJSON dictionary. We can inspect its structure and then convert it to a GeoDataFrame.

# Get the returned data in JSON format
# This is a dictionary
features = response.json()
type(features)

# What are the keys?
list(features.keys())

# Let's look at the first feature
features["features"][0]

# Create a GeoDataFrame
shootings = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(features, crs="EPSG:4326")
shootings.head()

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 3: Clean and Project

# Make sure we remove missing geometries
shootings = shootings.dropna(subset=["geometry"])

# Convert to a better CRS
shootings = shootings.to_crs(epsg=3857)

# Load city limits to clip the data
city_limits = gpd.read_file(
    "https://opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/405ec3da942d4e20869d4e1449a2be48_0.geojson"
).to_crs(epsg=3857)

# Remove any shootings that are outside the city limits
shootings = gpd.sjoin(
    shootings, city_limits, predicate="within", how="inner"
).drop(columns=["index_right"])

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 4: Visualisation
With the cleaned data in hand, we can produce two complementary visualisations: a point map and a hexbin map.

# From Open Data Philly
zip_codes = gpd.read_file(
    "https://opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/b54ec5210cee41c3a884c9086f7af1be_0.geojson"
).to_crs(epsg=3857)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))

# ZIP Codes
zip_codes.plot(ax=ax, facecolor="none", edgecolor="black")

# Shootings
shootings.plot(ax=ax, color="crimson", markersize=10, alpha=0.4)
ax.set_axis_off()


Hexbin Map
A hexbin map aggregates point events into hexagonal bins, revealing density patterns that are hard to see in a simple point map.

# Initialize the axes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10), facecolor=plt.get_cmap("viridis")(0))

# Convert to Web Mercator and plot the hexbins
x = shootings.geometry.x
y = shootings.geometry.y
ax.hexbin(x, y, gridsize=40, mincnt=1, cmap="viridis")

# Overlay the city limits
zip_codes.plot(ax=ax, facecolor="none", linewidth=0.5, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_axis_off()

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 5: Filtering with SQL
One of the strengths of the CARTO API is that you can filter on the server side using SQL.

# Example: Count the total number of rows in a table
response = requests.get(
    carto_api_endpoint, params={"q": "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shootings"}
)
response.json()

# Select nonfatal shootings only
query = "SELECT * FROM shootings WHERE fatal = 0"
params = {"q": query, "format": "geojson"}
response = requests.get(carto_api_endpoint, params=params)

# Make the GeoDataFrame
nonfatal = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(response.json(), crs="EPSG:4326")
print("number of nonfatal shootings = ", len(nonfatal))

# Select based on "date_"
query = "SELECT * FROM shootings WHERE date_ >= '1/1/23'"
params = {"q": query, "format": "geojson"}
response = requests.get(carto_api_endpoint, params=params)

# Make the GeoDataFrame
shootings_2023 = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(response.json(), crs="EPSG:4326")
print("number of shootings in 2023 = ", len(shootings_2023))

section: At-Home Exercise: Explore Trends by Month and Day of Week
text:
At-Home Exercise: Explore Trends by Month and Day of Week

# Convert the date column to a datetime object
shootings["date"] = pd.to_datetime(shootings["date_"])

# Add new columns: Month and Day of Week
shootings["Month"] = shootings["date"].dt.month
shootings["Day of Week"] = shootings["date"].dt.dayofweek  # Monday is 0, Sunday is 6

count = shootings.groupby(["Month", "Day of Week"]).size()
count = count.reset_index(name="Count")
count.head()


import hvplot.pandas

# Remember 0 is Monday and 6 is Sunday
count.hvplot.heatmap(
    x="Day of Week",
    y="Month",
    C="Count",
    cmap="viridis",
    width=400,
    height=500,
    flip_yaxis=True,
)







Key takeaway from Section 2



The CARTO example shows a more realistic API workflow: you construct query parameters, send a request with requests.get(), parse the JSON response, and convert it to a GeoDataFrame. This pattern appears in many geospatial web services.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Introduction
This part introduces two programmatic methods for downloading GIS layers from New Zealand’s national spatial data services: the Stats NZ Geographic Data Service (datafinder.stats.govt.nz) and the LINZ Data Service (data.linz.govt.nz). Rather than clicking through the web interface every time, you will write Python scripts that fetch, poll, and load geospatial data automatically. This is an essential habit in reproducible research: when your data acquisition step is scripted, anyone can re-run your entire workflow from scratch.
Both services are built on the Koordinates platform, which exposes a REST API. Every dataset you can browse in the web interface is also accessible programmatically using either of the two methods below.






Why programmatic download?



A manual download is fine for a one-off task, but it breaks reproducibility. If you are sharing your analysis through GitHub, a Quarto report, or a package, your collaborators cannot re-run the data acquisition step unless the exact same file is committed to the repository (which is impractical for large GIS files). A short script that downloads the data on demand is far more transparent and maintainable.



Methods covered








Method
Approach
Best for




Method A
Koordinates Export API
Saving a local GeoPackage or Shapefile; offline workflows


Method B
WFS (Web Feature Service)
Loading directly into a GeoDataFrame; spatial subsetting with a bounding box

section: Step 1: Create an Account and Obtain an API Key
text:
Step 1: Create an Account and Obtain an API Key
Both methods require a personal API key. Navigate to the Stats NZ Geographic Data Service and log in using your Koordinates ID. If you do not yet have one, click Sign Up on the login page.



Log in to Stats NZ Geographic Data Service using your Koordinates ID. If you do not have an account, click Sign Up to register.


Once logged in, go to:

https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/my/api/

Click Create API Key, give it a descriptive name (for example, GISCI343), and copy the key value. You will not be shown the full key again after navigating away from the page.






Keep your API key private



Your API key is a credential. Treat it like a password. Never paste it directly into a shared notebook or commit it to a public repository.
Store it in a separate file (for example config.py) that is listed in your .gitignore:
# config.py  ← add this filename to .gitignore
API_KEY = "your_key_here"
Then import it in your analysis script:
from config import API_KEY

title: Lab Week 04
section: Step 2: Find the Layer You Need
text:
Step 2: Find the Layer You Need
For this lab we will use the Regional Council 2025 Clipped layer (Layer ID: 120945), which contains the 17 regional boundaries of New Zealand.
Navigate to the layer page to review the metadata before downloading:

https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/layer/120945-regional-council-2025-clipped/

The homepage provides a search bar and a catalogue of all available datasets:



Stats NZ Geographic Data Service homepage — search for a dataset by name, or browse the Most Popular section.



Finding the Layer ID
Every API request requires the Layer ID, the integer that uniquely identifies a dataset. There are two ways to find it.
Method 1: Read it from the URL
When you open any layer page, the Layer ID is embedded directly in the browser address bar:
https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/layer/120945-regional-council-2025-clipped/
                                       ^^^^^^
                                       This is the Layer ID
Method 2: Read it from the Info tab
Open the layer page and make sure the Info tab is selected (it is the default). Scroll down below the thumbnail and you will see a metadata row showing Date Added, Last Updated, Views, Exports, and Layer ID. The number displayed there (e.g. 120945) is what you use in your script.



Two places the Layer ID appears: highlighted in the URL bar (top) and in the metadata row of the Info tab (bottom left).








Quick tip: search first, then check the URL



Search for the dataset you need using the search bar on the homepage. Once you have opened the correct layer page, copy the integer from the URL. It is always the first numeric segment after /layer/. You do not need to navigate anywhere else.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Method A: Koordinates Export API
The Export API creates a downloadable ZIP archive of a layer in a format and CRS of your choice. The workflow has three stages: create, poll, then download.
The settings you choose when calling the API mirror exactly what the web interface shows in the Export dialog:



Export dialog — the CRS dropdown, format selector, and layer checkbox correspond directly to the fields in the API request body.



Stage 1: Create the Export Job
Send a POST request with a JSON body specifying the layer URL, CRS, and file format. The Authorization header carries your API key.

import requests
import time
import zipfile
import io
import geopandas as gpd

from config import API_KEY  # store your key in config.py

LAYER_ID = 120945
BASE_URL = "https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/services/api/v1.x"

HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"key {API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type":  "application/json",
}

payload = {
    "crs":     "EPSG:2193",
    "formats": {"vector": "application/x-ogc-gpkg"},
    "items":   [{"item": f"{BASE_URL}/layers/{LAYER_ID}/"}],
}

response = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/exports/", json=payload, headers=HEADERS)
response.raise_for_status()

export_data = response.json()
export_url  = export_data["url"]
print(f"Export job created: {export_url}")
print(f"Current state: {export_data['state']}")







Available format strings






Format string
Output




application/x-ogc-gpkg
GeoPackage (recommended)


application/x-zipped-shp
Shapefile (ZIP)


application/json
GeoJSON


text/csv
CSV (attributes only, no geometry)







Stage 2: Poll Until Ready
The export is prepared asynchronously. Check the state field every few seconds until it returns "complete".

print("Waiting for export...", end="", flush=True)

while True:
    poll = requests.get(export_url, headers=HEADERS)
    poll.raise_for_status()
    state = poll.json()["state"]
    print(".", end="", flush=True)

    if state == "complete":
        download_url = poll.json()["download_url"]
        print(f"\nReady: {download_url}")
        break
    elif state in ("error", "cancelled"):
        raise RuntimeError(f"Export failed with state: {state}")

    time.sleep(5)



Stage 3: Download and Load
You can either save the ZIP to disk first, or extract it entirely in memory.

# --- Option 1: Save to disk ---
dl = requests.get(download_url, headers=HEADERS, stream=True)
dl.raise_for_status()

with open("regional_council_2025.zip", "wb") as f:
    for chunk in dl.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
        f.write(chunk)

with zipfile.ZipFile("regional_council_2025.zip") as zf:
    gpkg_name = [n for n in zf.namelist() if n.endswith(".gpkg")][0]
    zf.extractall("regional_council_2025/")

gdf = gpd.read_file(f"regional_council_2025/{gpkg_name}")
print(gdf.shape, gdf.crs)


# --- Option 2: Extract entirely in memory (no file saved) ---
dl2 = requests.get(download_url, headers=HEADERS)
with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(dl2.content)) as zf:
    gpkg_name = [n for n in zf.namelist() if n.endswith(".gpkg")][0]
    gdf = gpd.read_file(zf.open(gpkg_name))

print(gdf.shape, gdf.crs)
gdf.plot()

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Method B: WFS (Web Feature Service)
WFS is an OGC standard that lets you stream vector features directly into Python without downloading a ZIP. The endpoint is found under the Services and APIs tab on the layer page. Select WFS from the left-hand list and choose your API key from the dropdown.



Services and APIs tab — click WFS in the left panel to see the pre-filled endpoint URL and API key selector.



Read Directly into a GeoDataFrame
Construct the WFS URL and pass it directly to gpd.read_file(). GeoPandas fetches and parses the GeoJSON response automatically.

import geopandas as gpd
from config import API_KEY

LAYER_ID = 120945
wfs_base = f"https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/services;key={API_KEY}/wfs/"

params = (
    "service=WFS&version=2.0.0&request=GetFeature"
    f"&typeNames=layer-{LAYER_ID}"
    "&outputFormat=application/json"
    "&srsName=EPSG:2193"
)

gdf = gpd.read_file(f"{wfs_base}?{params}")
print(gdf.shape)   # (17, n_columns)
print(gdf.crs)     # EPSG:2193
gdf.plot(figsize=(8, 10))



Spatial Subsetting with a Bounding Box
For large layers, add a bbox parameter to retrieve only the features intersecting a defined area:

# Bounding box for Auckland region (EPSG:2193, metres)
# Format: min_easting, min_northing, max_easting, max_northing
bbox = "1730000,5900000,1820000,5990000"

params_bbox = (
    "service=WFS&version=2.0.0&request=GetFeature"
    f"&typeNames=layer-{LAYER_ID}"
    "&outputFormat=application/json&srsName=EPSG:2193"
    f"&bbox={bbox},EPSG:2193"
)

gdf_akl = gpd.read_file(f"{wfs_base}?{params_bbox}")
print(gdf_akl[["REGC2025_1", "LAND_AREA_SQ_KM"]])
gdf_akl.plot(figsize=(6, 6))







When should you use the bbox parameter?



The Regional Council layer only has 17 features, so bbox filtering saves little time here. However, for large layers such as meshblocks (~50,000 features) or building outlines (~3 million features), restricting to your study area makes a significant difference in download time and memory usage.

title: Lab Week 04
section: Applying the Same Methods to LINZ Data Service
text:
Applying the Same Methods to LINZ Data Service
The LINZ Data Service (data.linz.govt.nz) also runs on the Koordinates platform. This means the same two methods (Export API and WFS) work with only minor changes. You will need a separate API key from LINZ: sign up at data.linz.govt.nz, then go to My Account > API Keys and generate one.
In this section we will download NZ Building Outlines (All Sources) (Layer ID: 101292) and plot the results for Auckland city centre.

https://data.linz.govt.nz/layer/101292-nz-building-outlines-all-sources/







Large layers require spatial filtering



The NZ Building Outlines layer contains approximately 3 million features nationally. Downloading the full layer via WFS is impractical. Always use a bounding box or the Export API when working with large datasets like this.



LINZ WFS with Bounding Box
The LINZ WFS endpoint uses cql_filter with a bbox() function for spatial filtering, rather than the standard WFS bbox parameter. The geometry column for most LINZ layers is called shape.

import json
import requests
import geopandas as gpd
from config import LINZ_API_KEY  # store separately from Stats NZ key

LAYER_ID = 101292
WFS_URL = f"https://data.linz.govt.nz/services;key={LINZ_API_KEY}/wfs"

# Auckland city centre bounding box (EPSG:4326)
# min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat
BBOX = (174.7339, -36.8679, 174.8013, -36.8284)

params = {
    "service": "WFS",
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "request": "GetFeature",
    "typeNames": f"layer-{LAYER_ID}",
    "outputFormat": "application/json",
    "srsName": "EPSG:4326",
    "count": 50000,
    "cql_filter": (
        f"bbox(shape,{BBOX[0]},{BBOX[1]},{BBOX[2]},{BBOX[3]},'EPSG:4326')"
    ),
}

response = requests.get(WFS_URL, params=params, timeout=300)
response.raise_for_status()

geojson = response.json()
n_features = len(geojson.get("features", []))
print(f"Received {n_features} building outlines.")

# Save to file
with open("auckland_cbd_buildings.geojson", "w") as f:
    json.dump(geojson, f, indent=2)







Key differences between Stats NZ and LINZ WFS











Feature
Stats NZ
LINZ




Base URL
datafinder.stats.govt.nz
data.linz.govt.nz


API key
Stats NZ Koordinates account
LINZ Koordinates account


Spatial filter
Standard WFS bbox parameter
cql_filter=bbox(shape,...)


Default CRS
EPSG:2193 (NZTM)
EPSG:2193 (NZTM)







Plotting the Auckland City Centre Buildings
Once downloaded, load the GeoJSON into a GeoDataFrame and plot with a basemap for geographic context. The contextily library adds background map tiles automatically.

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

try:
    import contextily as cx
    HAS_BASEMAP = True
except ImportError:
    HAS_BASEMAP = False
    print("contextily not installed -- plotting without basemap.")
    print("Install with: pip install contextily")

gdf = gpd.read_file("auckland_cbd_buildings.geojson")
print(f"Loaded {len(gdf)} building outlines.")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 12))

if HAS_BASEMAP:
    # Reproject to Web Mercator for basemap tile alignment
    gdf_wm = gdf.to_crs(epsg=3857)
    gdf_wm.plot(
        ax=ax,
        facecolor="tomato",
        edgecolor="darkred",
        linewidth=0.15,
        alpha=0.5,
    )
    cx.add_basemap(ax, source=cx.providers.CartoDB.Positron, zoom=15)
    ax.set_axis_off()
else:
    gdf.plot(
        ax=ax,
        facecolor="steelblue",
        edgecolor="navy",
        linewidth=0.15,
        alpha=0.6,
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("Longitude")
    ax.set_ylabel("Latitude")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")

ax.set_title("Auckland City Centre Building Outlines (LINZ)", fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("auckland_cbd_buildings.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()



LINZ Export API
For the full national dataset, the Export API is the better option. The code is nearly identical to the Stats NZ version, with only the base URL and API key changed:

from config import LINZ_API_KEY

LAYER_ID = 101292
BASE_URL = "https://data.linz.govt.nz/services/api/v1"

HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"key {LINZ_API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

payload = {
    "crs": "EPSG:2193",
    "formats": {"vector": "application/x-ogc-gpkg"},
    "items": [{"item": f"{BASE_URL}/layers/{LAYER_ID}/"}],
}

response = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/exports/", json=payload, headers=HEADERS)
response.raise_for_status()

export_data = response.json()
export_url = export_data["url"]
print(f"Export job created: {export_url}")

# Poll and download using the same Stage 2 and Stage 3 code from Method A.
# Note: the full building outlines export may take several minutes and
# produce a file over 1 GB.

text:
Section 1: Assignment 2 briefing

The one-sentence version
By Sunday 10 May 2026, 23:59 NZST, you will publish a public shinylive dashboard, backed by a public GitHub repo, that addresses one urban or transport question about Auckland. A short design report (PDF rendered from Quarto) accompanies the code.
Assignment 2 is worth 15% of the course mark and is submitted via Canvas. Full brief in 3.6.






Random track assignment: 21 April, 13:10



You will be randomly assigned one of the three data tracks (Public Transport, Commuter + Student OD, or Auckland Crashes) on Tuesday 21 April 2026 at 13:10 NZST. Read all three in 3.6 before that date so you know what is coming.




What markers will look for
Look at the rubric in 3.6 before you start. The short version:

Question and framing is specific and defensible, scoped to your assigned track.
Data and methods are clean, documented, and reproducible.
Reactivity uses @reactive.calc correctly. No redundant computation. At least three user inputs actually change the outputs.
Map and visual design is readable and accessible. You have an ipyleaflet map (required) and a quantitative chart (Plotly or matplotlib).
Deployment to GitHub Pages works on a cold load, all controls respond.
Design report (under 4 pages, PDF rendered from Quarto) covers motivation, data, architecture, UI walkthrough, and limitations.



Preparing for the random track assignment
Your goal for today is to read all three tracks in 3.6 and note down one question you would ask within each. You will not know which one you get until 21 April, but if you have one sketch per track, the assignment day will not catch you off guard.
The three tracks and their datasets:

Track A: Public Transport. AT Data Sources (patronage) and AT GIS (buses, ferries).
Track B: Commuter + Student OD. Stats NZ Data Finder (2023 Census commuter and student datasets).
Track C: Auckland crashes. Where crashes are happening in Auckland.

title: Lab Week 06
text:
Section 2: Set up your project

Step 1: Create the project folder
Pick a sensible name. Your GitHub repo and your deployed URL will inherit it.
mkdir gisci343-a2-<your-topic>
cd gisci343-a2-<your-topic>

# Virtual environment
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Install Shiny
uv pip install shiny shinylive


Step 2: Scaffold with shiny create
Instead of a blank file, use Shiny’s generator:
shiny create
When prompted, pick basic-app (single file, one input, one output). Let it write into the current folder.
Run it:
shiny run --reload app.py
Open the URL Shiny prints in your browser. You should see a slider and a plot. Move the slider. The plot updates. Good: that confirms your install works.






Keep this habit



--reload watches your file. Save app.py in your editor and the app restarts automatically. You will save yourself dozens of restarts over the next three weeks.




Step 3: Initialise git and push to GitHub
You need to put your project under version control and push it to a public GitHub repository. There are two ways to do this: via GitHub Desktop (Option A, visual) or via the terminal (Option B, command line). Pick whichever you are more comfortable with; the end result is the same.






Set up GitHub authentication first



The push step below fails for most students if they have never authenticated git with GitHub on this laptop. Signing in to the GitHub website or GitHub Desktop is not enough: the git program itself needs its own credentials, either an SSH key or a personal access token over HTTPS.
If you have not done this yet, pause here and follow Section 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub first. It takes about five minutes and will save you from Permission denied (publickey) or Authentication failed errors in the next step.


Before either option, go to github.com and create a new empty public repository with the same name as your folder. Do not tick “Add a README” or “Add a .gitignore”, because shiny create has already produced those for you and the initial push will conflict otherwise.





flowchart LR
    A[Your laptop folder<br/>app.py, .venv, etc.] -->|git init<br/>or GitHub Desktop| B[Local git repo<br/>branch: main]
    B -->|stage + commit| C[First commit<br/>snapshot saved locally]
    C -->|connect remote| D[Linked to GitHub<br/>empty remote repo]
    D -->|push| E[Code on GitHub<br/>public URL]







Option A: GitHub Desktop (visual)Option B: Terminal (command line)


If you prefer a GUI, GitHub Desktop does all of the steps below with clicks instead of commands.
Visit here for any further information: https://docs.github.com/en/desktop
1. Add your existing folder to GitHub Desktop.
Open GitHub Desktop and go to File → Add Local Repository. Browse to your project folder (the one containing app.py). GitHub Desktop will detect that it is not yet a git repository and offer to initialise it for you. Click create a repository and accept the defaults.
2. Make your first commit.
GitHub Desktop will show all the files from shiny create in the Changes tab on the left. Each file is ticked (staged) by default. In the Summary box at the bottom left, type a message:
Initial scaffold from shiny create
Click Commit to main.
3. Publish to GitHub.
After the commit, a blue Publish repository button appears at the top. Click it. In the dialog:

Name: should already match your folder name.
Keep this code private: untick this (Assignment 2 needs a public repo).
Organisation: leave as your personal account.

Click Publish Repository. GitHub Desktop pushes everything to a new public repo on github.com.
4. Verify.
Click View on GitHub (or open https://github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo> in a browser). You should see app.py and the other files listed.


From your project folder, run:
# 1. Turn this folder into a git repo
git init

# 2. Stage everything that is not in .gitignore
git add .

# 3. Record the first snapshot
git commit -m "Initial scaffold from shiny create"

# 4. Rename the default branch to main (new repos sometimes default to master)
git branch -M main

# 5. Tell your local repo where the GitHub remote lives
#    Replace <your-username> and <your-repo> with your actual values
git remote add origin git@github.com:<your-username>/<your-repo>.git

# 6. Push your local main branch up, and set it to track the remote
git push -u origin main
After step 6, refresh your GitHub repo page. Your files should be there.









If the publish fails (GitHub Desktop) or the push is rejected (terminal)



Two common causes:

Authentication failure (Authentication failed in GitHub Desktop, Permission denied (publickey) in the terminal). Your git has no valid credentials for GitHub on this laptop. See Section 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub and set up a personal access token, then retry.
Non-empty remote repo. There is already a README on GitHub and your local main has unrelated history. In GitHub Desktop, start over with a fresh empty repo. From the terminal, pull first with git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories, resolve any conflicts, then push again.

title: Lab Week 06
section: Section 3: Build a one-page Shiny app
text:
Section 3: Build a one-page Shiny app
Replace the contents of app.py with the code below and save. The app shows a small table of Auckland suburbs, filtered by a minimum-population slider, and plots the median income of the surviving suburbs.
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Inline sample data (replace with real data next week)
suburbs = pd.DataFrame({
    "suburb":        ["Ponsonby", "Parnell", "Mt Eden", "Newmarket",
                      "Grey Lynn", "Remuera", "Onehunga", "Henderson"],
    "population":    [12500, 8900, 15300, 11200, 14800, 9600, 13500, 21000],
    "median_income": [75000, 95000, 68000, 82000, 71000, 105000, 58000, 52000],
})

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.h2("Auckland suburbs explorer"),
    ui.p("Filter suburbs by minimum population and see how incomes compare."),
    ui.input_slider("min_pop", "Minimum population", 0, 25000, 0, step=1000),
    ui.output_text("summary"),
    ui.output_table("tbl"),
    ui.output_plot("chart"),
)

def server(input, output, session):

    @reactive.calc
    def filtered():
        return suburbs[suburbs["population"] >= input.min_pop()]

    @render.text
    def summary():
        df = filtered()
        if len(df) == 0:
            return "No suburbs match the current filter."
        return f"{len(df)} suburbs, mean income ${df['median_income'].mean():,.0f}."

    @render.table
    def tbl():
        return filtered()

    @render.plot
    def chart():
        df = filtered()
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
        ax.barh(df["suburb"], df["median_income"], color="steelblue")
        ax.set_xlabel("Median income (NZ$)")
        ax.set_title("Median income by suburb")
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig

app = App(app_ui, server)
Save. Move the slider. The summary, table, and plot should all update together.

Checkpoint
Before moving on, convince yourself that you understand three things. If you cannot answer these out loud, re-read 3.1 before deploying.

Which lines are the UI, which lines are the server, and which line creates the App?
What happens if you remove the @reactive.calc and inline suburbs[suburbs["population"] >= input.min_pop()] in both tbl and chart? Does the app still work? Is it still efficient?
The summary and chart both read filtered(). If the slider moves, how many times does the filter actually run?







Try breaking it



Rename def tbl(): to def tabel(): and save. The table will disappear, but the app will not raise an error. Why? Fix it by matching the id in ui.output_table("tbl").

title: Lab Week 06
text:
Section 4: Deploy to GitHub Pages
This is the part most students underestimate. Leave yourself at least 30 minutes.
We will deploy straight from the main branch, using a docs/ folder. This is the simplest pattern: one branch, one push, and GitHub Pages serves the static build. (If you prefer the older gh-pages branch style, see the alternative at the bottom of this section.)





flowchart LR
    A[app.py<br/>on main] -->|shinylive export| B[docs/ folder<br/>static site]
    B -->|commit + push| C[main branch<br/>on GitHub]
    C -->|Pages: main /docs| D[Live URL<br/>username.github.io/repo]







Step 1: Export the app to static files
From your project folder, run:
shinylive export . docs
This reads app.py (and anything in the folder) and writes a static website to docs/. Open docs/index.html in your browser. Your app should run, with no Python server anywhere. If it does, your local export works.






Why docs/ and not site/?



GitHub Pages has built-in support for serving from a /docs folder on the main branch. Using that name means you only need to tick one box in Settings, no extra branch required.




Step 2: Commit the docs/ folder to main
You now need to add the new docs/ folder, commit it, and push it to GitHub. Pick the workflow you prefer.

Option A: GitHub Desktop (visual)Option B: Terminal (command line)


1. See the changes.
GitHub Desktop will show every file inside your new docs/ folder in the Changes tab on the left. There will be a lot of them (HTML, JS, WebAssembly bundles). That is normal.
2. Commit.
In the Summary box at the bottom left, type:
Deploy app to docs/
Click Commit to main.
3. Push.
At the top of the window, click Push origin. GitHub Desktop sends your commit up to the main branch on GitHub.
4. Verify.
Click View on GitHub (or open your repo in a browser). You should now see a docs/ folder at the top level.


# Stage the new docs/ folder
git add docs

# Commit
git commit -m "Deploy app to docs/"

# Push to main
git push origin main
Refresh your GitHub repo page. You should now see a docs/ folder at the top level.





Step 3: Enable GitHub Pages
In your repo on github.com:

Go to Settings → Pages.
Under Build and deployment → Source, pick Deploy from a branch.
Branch: main. Folder: /docs. Click Save.

Wait up to a minute. Your app will be live at:
https://<your-username>.github.io/<your-repo>/
First load is slow (10 to 30 seconds) because Pyodide and your packages have to download. Subsequent loads are fast, thanks to browser caching.






Redeploying after changes



Every time you change app.py, rerun shinylive export . docs, then commit and push. GitHub Pages will pick up the new build automatically, usually within a minute.

title: Lab Week 06
text:
Section 5: Homework and stretch goals

Minimum (everyone)
Before the Week 7 lab:

Replace the inline suburbs DataFrame with real data you actually want to use. A CSV, a GeoPackage, whatever fits your topic. Commit and redeploy.
Add a second input to your app: a dropdown, a date range, a checkbox group. Make an output depend on both.
Write two paragraphs in a README.md:

What question does this dashboard try to answer?
Where does the data come from?




Stretch (if you finish early)

Swap the @render.plot for an ipyleaflet map (see 3.4). Show your data on a real map tile layer.
Restructure the UI into a sidebar layout with ui.page_sidebar (see 3.3).
Add a @reactive.event button that recomputes only when clicked, rather than on every slider tick.



Common problems

shinylive export succeeds but the deployed app shows a blank page. Check the browser Console (Cmd + Option + I on macOS, F12 on Windows and Linux). Usually a missing package or a path-case mismatch.
GitHub Pages says “404” for a minute after enabling. This is normal. Refresh after 60 seconds.
The first load takes forever. This is Pyodide downloading. Subsequent loads are fast. If you want to tell users to wait, add a note in your UI.
folium does not work after deploy. Correct: folium is not in Pyodide. Use ipyleaflet instead (see 3.4).



Submission
No formal submission this week. Check-in is your public URL, posted in Slack. We will use it as the starting point for the Week 7 lab.

Where to write the plan

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 1: Motivation and audience (30 min)
Answer the following questions in two to four paragraphs. Be specific; “Auckland residents” is too broad.

1.1 What problem does your dashboard address?
State the question your dashboard will help someone answer. Good questions are narrow enough that a single dashboard can answer them convincingly:

Track A example: “How has public transport patronage in Auckland recovered since 2020, and which modes are recovering fastest?”
Track B example: “Do workers and university students from the same origin SA2 commute to the same destinations, or do their travel patterns diverge?”
Track C example: “Where in Auckland are serious and fatal crashes concentrated, and has the spatial pattern shifted over the past five years?”

Write your own question. Do not copy the examples above.


1.2 Who is it for?
Describe one or two realistic users. What role do they hold? What decision would this dashboard inform? For example, a transport planner at Auckland Transport evaluating whether to increase frequency on a bus route, or a public health researcher comparing active-transport crash risk across suburbs.


1.3 What insight does it enable?
In one sentence, state the single most important thing a user should take away after spending two minutes with your dashboard. This sentence will likely become the title or subtitle of your app.






Why this matters for the rubric



The “Question” criterion (10%) rewards dashboards that address a clear, well-scoped question. Writing it down now, before you touch the code, prevents the common mistake of building a dashboard that shows data but does not answer anything.

2.2 Cleaning and preparation steps
For each dataset, list the steps you need to take before it is ready for the app. Be concrete:

Which columns will you keep? Which will you drop?
Do you need to melt, pivot, merge, or aggregate?
What is the original CRS? Do you need to reproject to EPSG:4326 for ipyleaflet?
Do you need to simplify geometries to keep the file size small for shinylive?

Write this as a numbered list. Each step should be one line.


2.3 Limitations
Every dataset has gaps. Note at least two limitations, for example: “Patronage data is monthly, so I cannot show weekly patterns” or “The crash dataset does not distinguish between crashes involving cyclists and those involving e-scooter riders”.
Acknowledging limitations early shows the marker that you understand your data, and it will become a paragraph in your design report.






Do the preparation now, not later



Open your dataset in a notebook. Run .head(), .dtypes, .columns, .shape. Fill in the table above with actual column names and row counts, not guesses. If the data is not what you expected, now is the time to find a better source or adjust your question.

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 3: Technical architecture (30 min)

3.1 App structure
Sketch the layout of your app. Which layout will you use: ui.page_sidebar, ui.page_navbar, or something else? List the panels or pages and what goes in each one.
Example (do not copy, write your own):
page_sidebar
  sidebar:
    - input_select: origin SA2
    - input_checkbox_group: population (worker, student)
    - input_slider: top N destinations
  main area:
    - card: bar chart of top destinations
    - card: ipyleaflet map highlighting destination SA2s


3.2 Reactive dependency diagram
Draw a Mermaid diagram showing how your inputs flow through reactive calculations to outputs. Paste this into your plan.qmd (or plan.md) so it renders when you preview it.
Here is a template to adapt (replace the node labels with your actual input/output names):
```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A["input.origin()"] --> D["@reactive.calc<br/>filtered()"]
    B["input.pops()"] --> D
    C["input.top_n()"] --> D
    D --> E["@render.plot<br/>chart"]
    D --> F["@render_widget<br/>map"]
    D --> G["@render.text<br/>summary"]
```
Your diagram must include:

All three required inputs (with their ui.input_* type).
At least one @reactive.calc that is shared by two or more outputs.
The map output (@render_widget) and the chart output (@render.plot or @render_widget).



3.3 Key functions
List the two or three most important functions you will write (besides the ones Shiny gives you). For each one, write a one-line docstring. For example:

prep_patronage(raw_df, modes, year_from): filter patronage data by selected modes and start year, return a tidy DataFrame.
colour_by_severity(severity): return a hex colour string for a crash severity level.



3.4 Performance considerations
shinylive runs in the browser via Pyodide. Large files and heavy computation will make the app slow to load. Note any steps you will take to keep things fast:

Target file size for data/ folder (aim for under 2 MB total).
Geometry simplification tolerance.
Whether you will cap the number of rendered map markers.
Whether you will use @reactive.event to gate an expensive calculation behind a button.

Start your skeleton app
If you still have time, open app.py and replace the hello-world content with your planned layout. You do not need working data yet; placeholder text is fine:
from shiny import App, ui, render

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_select("placeholder_1", "Input 1", choices=["a", "b"]),
        ui.input_slider("placeholder_2", "Input 2", 0, 100, 50),
        ui.input_checkbox_group("placeholder_3", "Input 3",
                                choices=["x", "y"], selected=["x"]),
    ),
    ui.card(ui.card_header("Chart"), ui.output_plot("chart")),
    ui.card(ui.card_header("Map"), "Map will go here"),
    title="My A2 dashboard",
)

def server(input, output, session):
    @render.plot
    def chart():
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.text(0.5, 0.5, "chart placeholder", ha="center", va="center")
        ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
        return fig

app = App(app_ui, server)
Run it with shiny run --reload app.py to confirm the layout matches your plan. Swap in real data next week.

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 3: Technical architecture
This section asks you to describe what a user sees and does when they open your finished dashboard. Write this in your plan.md as a short narrative (three to five paragraphs). Reading your narrative, a classmate who has never seen your data should be able to picture the dashboard in their head.
Below are three example narratives, one per track. Read the one for your track carefully, then write your own version that matches your specific question, your actual column names, and your design choices.

Track A: Public TransportTrack B: Commuter and Student ODTrack C: Auckland Crashes


When the user opens the dashboard, they see a sidebar on the left and two cards on the right. The title reads something like “Auckland PT Patronage Explorer”.
In the sidebar, a checkbox group lists the transport modes available in the patronage dataset (for example, Bus, Train, Ferry). All modes are selected by default. Below that, a slider sets the start year: the user can drag it from, say, 2014 to 2024 to zoom in on recent trends. At the bottom of the sidebar, an “Apply filters” button lets the user adjust both controls before anything recalculates.
The top card holds a line chart (matplotlib or Plotly). Each selected mode appears as a separate line, with months on the x-axis and total boardings on the y-axis. When the user deselects “Ferry”, the ferry line disappears and the y-axis rescales to make bus and train trends easier to compare.
The bottom card holds an ipyleaflet map of Auckland, centred around the CBD. Bus or ferry route geometries are drawn as coloured lines on the map. If the user has deselected a mode, those routes disappear from the map as well. Optionally, a dropdown in the sidebar could let the user pick a single route to highlight in red while the rest are dimmed to grey, so they can trace one route across the city.
A one-line text summary sits between the two cards: “Showing 1,240 monthly records across 2 modes from 2018 onward.” This updates whenever the user clicks “Apply filters”.


When the user opens the dashboard, they see a sidebar on the left and two cards on the right. The title reads something like “Where do Auckland workers and students go?”
In the sidebar, a dropdown lists the SA2 areas in Auckland. The user picks one as the origin (for example, “Ponsonby”). Below that, a checkbox group with two options, “Worker” and “Student”, controls which population is included. Both are selected by default so the user sees a side-by-side comparison. A slider sets how many top destinations to show (for example, 5 to 30, defaulting to 10). An “Apply filters” button sits at the bottom.
The top card holds a horizontal bar chart. Each bar is a destination SA2, sorted by flow count. If both populations are selected, worker and student bars appear side by side in different colours so the user can immediately see where the two groups diverge. Selecting only “Student” removes the worker bars and re-sorts.
The bottom card holds an ipyleaflet map. The origin SA2 is highlighted in green. The top-N destination SA2s are shaded in blue, with darker fills for higher flow counts. When the user switches the origin dropdown to a different suburb, both the chart and the map redraw to show the new origin’s commuting pattern.
A one-line text summary reads: “From Ponsonby: 3,450 workers and 820 students travel to 10 destinations.” This updates on each “Apply filters” click.


When the user opens the dashboard, they see a sidebar on the left and two cards on the right. The title reads something like “Auckland Crash Explorer”.
In the sidebar, a range slider sets the year window (for example, 2019 to 2024). Below that, a checkbox group lists severity levels (Fatal, Serious, Minor, Non-injury), all selected by default. A second checkbox group lists the travel modes involved (for example, Pedestrian, Cyclist, Motorcyclist, Driver). An “Apply filters” button sits at the bottom.
The top card holds an ipyleaflet map of Auckland. Each crash is a small coloured dot: dark red for fatal, bright red for serious, orange for minor, pale for non-injury. The dots update when the user clicks “Apply filters”. Because there may be thousands of points, only the first 2,000 are rendered (the text summary warns the user if records were capped). Zooming in on a neighbourhood lets the user see individual crash locations.
The bottom card holds a stacked bar chart with one bar per year. Each bar is segmented by severity, so the user can see whether serious crashes are increasing, decreasing, or steady. Deselecting “Non-injury” from the checkbox removes that segment and makes the serious/fatal proportions easier to read.
A one-line text summary reads: “4,312 crashes match the current filters (capped at 2,000 on the map). 87 fatal, 410 serious.” This updates on each “Apply filters” click.




What to write in your plan
After reading the narrative above for your track, write your own version in plan.md. Your narrative should mention:

The layout you will use (sidebar, navbar, or something else).
Every input by name and type (dropdown, slider, checkbox group, button).
Every output by type (map, chart, text summary) and what it shows.
What changes when the user interacts: which outputs redraw, and why.

You do not need to write code yet. That comes in Section 4.


3.2 Reactive dependency diagram

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 4: ipyleaflet maps inside Shiny
Now that the plan is written, start building. This section shows you how to get an ipyleaflet map into your Shiny app for each track. All examples use indicative column names; adapt them to your actual data.

The basic pattern
Every track uses the same wiring. In the UI, use output_widget from shinywidgets. In the server, use @render_widget and return a new Map object each time the reactive inputs change.
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
from shinywidgets import output_widget, render_widget
from ipyleaflet import Map, GeoData
import geopandas as gpd

gdf = gpd.read_file("data/your_file.geojson").to_crs(4326)

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_select("category", "Category",
                        choices=["All"] + sorted(gdf["category"].unique().tolist())),
    ),
    output_widget("map"),
    title="My dashboard",
)

def server(input, output, session):

    @reactive.calc
    def filtered():
        if input.category() == "All":
            return gdf
        return gdf[gdf["category"] == input.category()]

    @render_widget
    def map():
        m = Map(center=(-36.85, 174.77), zoom=11)
        m.add_layer(GeoData(
            geo_dataframe=filtered(),
            style={"color": "#1f78b4", "weight": 2, "fillOpacity": 0.4},
        ))
        return m

app = App(app_ui, server)
Two rules that prevent silent failures:

Always .to_crs(4326) when you load the GeoDataFrame. ipyleaflet expects WGS84; NZTM data will render as an empty map with no error.
Return a new Map() inside @render_widget every time. Do not create the Map at module level and try to mutate it; the widget will not update.


Track A: Public TransportTrack B: Commuter and Student ODTrack C: Auckland Crashes


Your map should show bus or ferry routes (lines). Use GeoData with a LineString GeoDataFrame. Wire a checkbox_group for transport modes so the user can toggle bus, train, and ferry layers.
from ipyleaflet import Map, GeoData
import geopandas as gpd

routes = gpd.read_file("data/routes.geojson").to_crs(4326)

@reactive.calc
def filtered_routes():
    return routes[routes["mode"].isin(input.modes())]

@render_widget
def map():
    m = Map(center=(-36.85, 174.77), zoom=11)
    sub = filtered_routes()
    if not sub.empty:
        m.add_layer(GeoData(
            geo_dataframe=sub,
            style={"color": "#d73027", "weight": 2, "opacity": 0.7},
            name="Routes",
        ))
    return m
To highlight a single route selected from a dropdown, add a second GeoData layer in a different colour:
@render_widget
def map():
    m = Map(center=(-36.85, 174.77), zoom=11)
    # all routes, dimmed
    m.add_layer(GeoData(
        geo_dataframe=filtered_routes(),
        style={"color": "#bdbdbd", "weight": 1, "opacity": 0.4},
    ))
    # selected route, bright
    sel = filtered_routes()
    sel = sel[sel["route_short_name"] == input.route()]
    if not sel.empty:
        m.add_layer(GeoData(
            geo_dataframe=sel,
            style={"color": "#e31a1c", "weight": 4, "opacity": 1.0},
        ))
    return m


Your map should show destination polygons (SA2 areas). Use GeoData with a Polygon GeoDataFrame. Highlight the origin SA2 in one colour and the top-N destinations in another.
from ipyleaflet import Map, GeoData
import geopandas as gpd

sa2 = gpd.read_file("data/sa2_auckland.geojson").to_crs(4326)

@reactive.calc
def dest_areas():
    # top_codes is a list of SA2 codes from the OD filter
    top_codes = filtered_od()["dest"].unique()
    return sa2[sa2["SA2_code"].isin(top_codes)]

@render_widget
def map():
    m = Map(center=(-36.85, 174.77), zoom=10)
    # highlight origin
    origin = sa2[sa2["SA2_code"] == input.origin()]
    if not origin.empty:
        m.add_layer(GeoData(
            geo_dataframe=origin,
            style={"color": "#2ca25f", "fillColor": "#99d8c9",
                   "fillOpacity": 0.6, "weight": 3},
            name="Origin",
        ))
    # highlight destinations
    dests = dest_areas()
    if not dests.empty:
        m.add_layer(GeoData(
            geo_dataframe=dests,
            style={"color": "#1f78b4", "fillColor": "#a6cee3",
                   "fillOpacity": 0.5, "weight": 1},
            name="Destinations",
        ))
    return m


Your map should show crash points. Use CircleMarker for each row. Colour by severity. Cap the number of markers to keep the browser responsive.
from ipyleaflet import Map, CircleMarker, LayerGroup

@render_widget
def map():
    df = filtered_crashes().head(2000)  # cap for performance
    severity_colours = {
        "Fatal": "#b10026",
        "Serious": "#e31a1c",
        "Minor": "#fd8d3c",
        "Non-injury": "#fee8c8",
    }
    markers = []
    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        markers.append(CircleMarker(
            location=(row.geometry.y, row.geometry.x),
            radius=4,
            color=severity_colours.get(row["severity"], "#636363"),
            fill_color=severity_colours.get(row["severity"], "#636363"),
            fill_opacity=0.7,
            weight=1,
        ))
    m = Map(center=(-36.85, 174.77), zoom=11)
    m.add_layer(LayerGroup(layers=tuple(markers)))
    return m






Why .head(2000)?



Each CircleMarker is a separate JavaScript object in the browser. Rendering 20,000 of them will freeze the page. Start with 2,000 and increase only if performance is acceptable. For the final submission, consider aggregating to a grid or using a heatmap layer instead.

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 5: Adding an action button
An action button lets the user control when an expensive operation runs, instead of the app recalculating on every slider tick. This is the @reactive.event pattern from the lecture.

Step 1: Add the button to the UI
Place it at the bottom of your sidebar, after all the filter inputs:
ui.sidebar(
    ui.input_select("category", "Category", choices=[...]),
    ui.input_slider("min_value", "Minimum", 0, 100, 0),
    ui.input_checkbox_group("modes", "Modes", choices=[...]),
    ui.input_action_button("apply", "Apply filters"),
)


Step 2: Gate the reactive calc
Wrap your shared @reactive.calc with @reactive.event so it only recalculates when the button is clicked:
@reactive.calc
@reactive.event(input.apply)
def filtered():
    df = data.copy()
    if input.category() != "All":
        df = df[df["category"] == input.category()]
    df = df[df["value"] >= input.min_value()]
    return df
Now the user can adjust multiple inputs, then click “Apply filters” once. The map and chart update together, and only once.


Step 3: Add a reset button (optional but useful)
# In the UI, next to the apply button:
ui.input_action_button("reset", "Reset"),

# In the server:
@reactive.effect
@reactive.event(input.reset)
def _():
    ui.update_select("category", selected="All")
    ui.update_slider("min_value", value=0)
    ui.update_checkbox_group("modes", selected=modes)
ui.update_* functions push new values into the inputs from the server side. Combined with @reactive.event, the reset click restores defaults and the apply click picks them up.


Step 4: Show a summary line
Add a text output that tells the user what the current filter produced:
# UI
ui.output_text("summary"),

# Server
@render.text
def summary():
    df = filtered()
    return f"{len(df):,} records match the current filters."
Because summary reads filtered(), it updates whenever the “Apply filters” button fires, not on every slider move. No extra wiring needed.

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Lab Objectives
By the end of this lab you will:

Write a short planning document that describes your dashboard’s purpose, audience, and data — this feeds directly into your design report.
Understand how @reactive.calc, @reactive.effect, and filtering fit together in a Shiny app.
Render a working ipyleaflet map inside a Shiny app.

What you need:

Your track assignment confirmed (Track A, B, or C).
Your own dataset downloaded from the sources listed in 3.6 and saved under data/.
The Week 6 repo with a working hello-world Shiny app.







Where to write your plan



Create a file called plan.md (or plan.qmd) in the root of your project repo. You will copy the best parts of this into your design report later.

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 3: Technical Planning
Write a short narrative (three to five paragraphs) in your plan.md describing what a user sees and does when they open your dashboard. A classmate who has never seen your data should be able to picture it after reading.

What a good narrative covers

The layout (sidebar, navbar, or something else).
Every input by name and type (dropdown, slider, checkbox group, action button).
Every output by type (map, chart, text summary) and what it shows.
What changes when the user interacts.



Example narrative (generic)

When the user opens the dashboard, they see a sidebar on the left and two cards on the right. The title reads “Auckland Explorer”.
In the sidebar, a dropdown lets the user pick a category. A slider sets a minimum value. An “Apply filters” button sits at the bottom — the user adjusts both controls first, then clicks once to update everything.
The top card shows a chart that updates to reflect the filtered data. The bottom card shows an ipyleaflet map with the filtered records plotted as points or polygons. A one-line text summary between the two cards reads: “Showing 1,240 records matching the current filters.”



Key functions to plan for
When you plan your app, think about where each of these will appear:

@reactive.calc — a shared filtered dataset that multiple outputs depend on. Define it once; your chart and map both call it. This avoids filtering the data twice.
@reactive.effect — side effects that do not return a value, such as resetting inputs when the user clicks a “Reset” button.
Filtering — the logic inside your @reactive.calc that subsets rows based on the current input values (selected category, slider range, checkbox selection, and so on).

You do not need to write code yet. Write the narrative first, then identify which of the functions above you will use and where.

title: Lab Week 07
text:
Section 4: ipyleaflet Map inside Shiny
Here we provide a tiny complete, working example using data/NX2.gpkg — the NX2 Northern Express bus route from Hibiscus Coast Station to Auckland Universities. Run it as-is to see a working map, then adapt it to your own dataset.
Follow the link to Canvas for Week 7.
Unzip the file.
Now start building.
The dataset has one row (the full route geometry as a MultiLineString) and average daily boardings for each day of the week (Mon_av through Sun_av). The app lets the user pick a day and shows the route coloured by weekday vs weekend, with a summary of average boardings.
In a separate folder, launch uv and download the relevant packages shiny, shinywidgets, ipyleaflet, and geopandas. It is always good to run a fresh new uv environment!
uv venv

source .venv/bin/activate # MacOSX
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 # Windows PowerShell

uv pip install shiny shinywidgets ipyleaflet geopandas
Once you see that the uv is activated, go and check your app.py. It may look like below:
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
from shinywidgets import output_widget, render_widget
from ipyleaflet import Map, GeoData
import geopandas as gpd

# Load once at module level — always reproject to EPSG:4326 for ipyleaflet
route = gpd.read_file("data/NX2.gpkg", layer="bus_route").to_crs(4326)

day_labels = {
    "Mon_av": "Monday",
    "Tue_av": "Tuesday",
    "Wed_av": "Wednesday",
    "Thu_av": "Thursday",
    "Fri_av": "Friday",
    "Sat_av": "Saturday",
    "Sun_av": "Sunday",
}

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_select("day", "Day of week", choices=day_labels),
        ui.input_action_button("apply", "Apply"),
        width=250,
    ),
    ui.output_text("summary"),
    output_widget("map"),
    title="NX2 Bus Route Explorer",
)

def server(input, output, session):

    @reactive.calc
    @reactive.event(input.apply, ignore_none=False)
    def selected_day():
        # Returns the chosen column name; outputs read from it
        return input.day()

    @reactive.effect
    @reactive.event(input.apply)
    def _():
        # Side effect: log to console on each apply click
        col = selected_day()
        boardings = int(route[col].iloc[0])
        print(f"Day: {day_labels[col]}, avg boardings: {boardings:,}")

    @render.text
    def summary():
        col = selected_day()
        boardings = int(route[col].iloc[0])
        return f"NX2 average boardings on {day_labels[col]}: {boardings:,}"

    @render_widget
    def map():
        col = selected_day()
        weekdays = {"Mon_av", "Tue_av", "Wed_av", "Thu_av", "Fri_av"}
        colour = "#d73027" if col in weekdays else "#1f78b4"
        m = Map(center=(-36.74, 174.72), zoom=11)
        m.add_layer(GeoData(
            geo_dataframe=route,
            style={"color": colour, "weight": 4, "opacity": 0.8},
            name="NX2 route",
        ))
        return m

app = App(app_ui, server)
Now, run the app using the play button on the top left of the app.py file. Alternatively, you can run the app in your uv terminal using shiny run --reload app.py and follow the instructions.
Two rules that prevent silent failures:

Always .to_crs(4326) when loading a GeoDataFrame. ipyleaflet expects WGS84; NZTM data (EPSG:2193) will render as an empty map with no error message.
Return a new Map() inside @render_widget every time. Do not create the map at module level and try to mutate it; the widget will not update.


Your task
Adapt the example above to your own dataset and track. For more working code patterns, browse the Python Shiny gallery — every example includes full source code you can copy and modify.

text:
What you will learn
Your dashboard works. The slider moves, the map updates, the filter is correct. That gets you about 60% of the assignment marks. The remaining 40% — UI polish, deployment, and not falling over when someone touches the wrong button — is what this section is for.
This is the last lecture of Part 3. Two hours: one on polish (making the app look like a tool a stranger would trust), one on ship (making it survive contact with users and shinylive). Everything here applies directly to the rubric in 3.7.
We will keep extending the suburbs explorer from 3.3 — same data, same logic, only the UI and the robustness change.

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
section: Why polish matters for the design report
text:
Why polish matters for the design report
The Assignment 2 rubric (3.7) gives 20% to “Map and visual design” and another 5% to “UI polish and documentation”. The “User interface design” section asks for clean, logically organised, clearly labelled, readable without clutter. None of that is vanity. A dashboard that looks unfinished signals to a marker that the analysis behind it might also be unfinished. Polish is part of the argument.
The good news: the difference between a default Shiny app and a presentable one is roughly thirty minutes of work, and most of those minutes are spent picking colours.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
section: bslib: themes you can actually customise
text:
bslib: themes you can actually customise
shinyswatch (3.3) gives you a fixed list of pre-baked themes. Useful, but they all look like everyone else’s. bslib is the layer underneath: it lets you set the primary colour, the background, the font, and the spacing without writing CSS.
bslib ships with Shiny for Python — no extra install.
from shiny import ui
from shiny.ui import bslib

theme = bslib.bs_theme(
    bg="#fdfdfd",          # page background
    fg="#1f2937",          # body text
    primary="#0d6efd",     # buttons, links, sliders
    base_font=["Inter", "sans-serif"],
)

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(...),
    ...,
    title="Suburbs explorer",
    theme=theme,
)
Four arguments cover 90% of what you will want:



Argument
Controls




bg
Page background colour


fg
Default text colour


primary
Buttons, links, slider tracks, active tab indicators


base_font
Font stack (first available wins)



Pick a primary that matches your dataset’s domain — green for parks, red for crashes, blue for transit. Stick with one. Mixing accent colours mid-app reads as noise.






Use a real font



base_font=["Inter", "sans-serif"] looks markedly better than the browser default. Inter is widely available; if it is not on the user’s system, the browser falls back to sans-serif.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
section: Value boxes for the headline numbers
text:
Value boxes for the headline numbers
A value box is a card with one big number and a label. Three of them across the top of a dashboard is the cheapest “executive summary” you can build.
from shiny import ui

ui.layout_columns(
    ui.value_box(
        "Suburbs",
        ui.output_text("vb_count"),
        showcase=ui.tags.i(class_="bi bi-map"),
        theme="primary",
    ),
    ui.value_box(
        "Mean income",
        ui.output_text("vb_mean"),
        showcase=ui.tags.i(class_="bi bi-cash-stack"),
        theme="success",
    ),
    ui.value_box(
        "Highest income",
        ui.output_text("vb_max"),
        showcase=ui.tags.i(class_="bi bi-graph-up"),
        theme="warning",
    ),
    col_widths=[4, 4, 4],
)
In the server, each vb_* output is just a @render.text reading the same filtered() calc you already have:
@render.text
def vb_count():
    return f"{len(filtered()):,}"

@render.text
def vb_mean():
    return f"${filtered()['median_income'].mean():,.0f}"
The icons are Bootstrap Icons, bundled with Shiny. Browse the gallery, paste the class name, done.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
section: Richer cards: headers, footers, full screen
text:
Richer cards: headers, footers, full screen
ui.card already has a card_header. It also has a card_footer (good for source attributions) and a full_screen=True flag that gives the user an expand button. For dense charts and maps, that one flag massively improves usability:
ui.card(
    ui.card_header("Auckland parks"),
    output_widget("parks_map"),
    ui.card_footer(
        ui.tags.small("Source: Auckland Council Open Data, 2024"),
    ),
    full_screen=True,
)

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
text:
Tooltips, popovers, and help text
The rubric explicitly mentions “help text”. You do not need a paragraph; you need a hint next to each non-obvious control.
ui.tooltip(
    ui.input_slider("min_pop", "Minimum population", 0, 25000, 0),
    "Suburbs below this population are hidden from the chart and table.",
)
For longer help (one or two sentences), use a popover triggered by a small info icon:
ui.popover(
    ui.tags.i(class_="bi bi-info-circle"),
    "We exclude suburbs with fewer than 50 dwellings to avoid noise.",
    title="About this filter",
)
Place these next to the inputs they explain, not in a separate “Help” tab. Discoverability beats completeness.

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
text:
Loading states and busy indicators
When a @reactive.calc takes more than half a second, the app feels broken. Show that something is happening.
The simplest pattern, available in recent Shiny versions, is one line at the top of your UI:
app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.busy_indicators.use(),
    ...,
)
This adds a small pulsing indicator on every output that is currently recomputing. No code changes elsewhere.
For genuinely long operations (loading a 50 MB GeoPackage, running a clustering routine), use ui.Progress for an explicit bar:
@reactive.calc
def heavy_compute():
    with ui.Progress(min=0, max=3) as p:
        p.set(1, message="Loading data")
        df = pd.read_parquet("data/big.parquet")
        p.set(2, message="Aggregating")
        result = df.groupby("suburb").size()
        p.set(3, message="Done")
        return result
Progress messages are visible to the user. Use them for steps that are actually slow, not for atmosphere.

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
section: File size: GeoJSON is the wrong format
text:
File size: GeoJSON is the wrong format
The 5 MB rule from 3.5 cuts harder than it sounds. GeoJSON is plain text — every coordinate is stored as a 15-character decimal. GeoParquet stores the same geometry as binary floats, typically 5-10x smaller, and GeoPandas reads it just as easily.
Pre-process once, ship the small file:
# Run this once, locally, NOT inside your app
import geopandas as gpd

parks = gpd.read_file("auckland_parks_full.geojson")
parks = parks[["name", "area_ha", "geometry"]]                # drop unused columns
parks["geometry"] = parks.geometry.simplify(0.0001)           # simplify to ~10m
parks.to_parquet("data/parks.parquet")                        # binary, small
Tolerances for simplify (in EPSG:4326 degrees, since you are reprojecting for ipyleaflet anyway):

0.00001 — preserves shape almost perfectly, modest savings.
0.0001 — Auckland-scale, suburb-level shapes still readable.
0.001 — region-level only; suburbs become unrecognisable.

Start at 0.0001, eyeball the result on a map, increase if you can stomach the loss.

title: 3.6. Polish and Ship
section: Shinylive build and GitHub Pages debugging
text:
Shinylive build and GitHub Pages debugging
The assignment requires shinylive on GitHub Pages. We are not covering shinyapps.io or Posit Connect — they are out of scope for this course. What follows is the troubleshooting checklist for the deployment path you have to use.

The five failures that get reported in office hours
1. “ImportError: No module named X” in the browser console.
Pyodide does not have every package. Check the table in 3.4. The frequent offenders: folium, r5py, anything with C extensions outside the Pyodide list. Switch to a Pyodide-supported equivalent or precompute the result and ship the answer rather than the calculation.
2. “FileNotFoundError” for a file that exists locally.
Your read_file("/Users/me/project/data/x.geojson") worked locally. It fails in the browser because there is no /Users/me/. Use paths relative to app.py:
gpd.read_file("data/x.geojson")     # good
gpd.read_file("./data/x.geojson")   # also good
3. The deployed app loads, but the data is missing.
shinylive export only bundles files inside the app folder. If your data lives in a sibling folder, move it or symlink it. Check the contents of docs/ after export — every data file should be there.
4. GitHub Pages serves the repo root, not your docs/ folder.
Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from a branch → Branch: main, Folder: /docs. Save. Wait one minute. The URL is https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/, not https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/docs/.
5. The app works locally but breaks in the browser.
Open the browser console (3.1: F12 on Windows, ⌥⌘I on macOS). Pyodide errors show up there in red, with a stack trace. Read the trace from the bottom up — the topmost frame is usually the line in your app.py that triggered the failure.


Pre-submission checklist
Before your final git push, walk through this list:

App loads at the public URL on a cold browser (incognito mode).
All inputs cause a visible change in at least one output.
Empty-state behaviour: every extreme slider position, every “no selection” dropdown still renders something sensible.
Total size of data/ is under 5 MB.
README explains: what the dashboard answers, where the data came from, how to run it locally.
requirements.txt or pyproject.toml lists every package you import.
The deployed URL is in your repo description.
You have opened the deployed URL on a phone — at least the layout does not break.
The design report (3.7 deliverable) has been rendered to PDF and renamed to the required filename.

bslib.bs_theme() gives you four knobs that cover most theming work.
ui.value_box, ui.tooltip, ui.popover, and ten lines of CSS lift the visual standard significantly.
ui.busy_indicators.use() adds loading states everywhere with one line.
req, explicit empty-state UI, and try / except with ui.notification_show make your reactives safe.
Module-level loading + @reactive.calc is the right performance pattern; re-reading data inside renderers is the wrong one.
GeoParquet is much smaller than GeoJSON for the same data.
The five common shinylive failures are all visible in the browser console.

section: Part 1: Why Packaging Matters for GIScience
text:
Part 1: Why Packaging Matters for GIScience

The Research Reality
Without packages: - 📂 5 projects, 5 copies of the same CRS validation function - 🐛 Find a bug? Fix it in 5 places (and remember where they all are) - 🤝 Collaborator wants your code? Send a zip file and hope it works - 📊 Reproduce analysis? “Which version did I use again?”
With packages: - ✅ One function, maintained in one place - ✅ Fix once, improves everywhere - ✅ Share with pip install your-package - ✅ Pin version: your-package==1.2.0 ensures reproducibility


Real-World GIScience Use Cases
1. Research Lab Toolkit
Instead of:
# Everyone has their own version
from utils import calculate_accessibility  # Which utils?
Use:
pip install lab-spatial-toolkit==2.1.0
from lab_spatial_toolkit import calculate_accessibility
2. Course Infrastructure
Instead of:
# Students struggle with data loading
gdf = gpd.read_file('../../data/maybe/here/boundaries.gpkg')
Use:
pip install gisci343-toolkit
from gisci343_toolkit import load_assignment_data
pedestrians, boundaries = load_assignment_data(assignment=2)
3. Consulting Deliverable
Instead of: - Send zip file - Hope they have the right Python version - Hope they install dependencies correctly - Cross fingers
Use:
# In your project report:
# "To reproduce: pip install auckland-transport-analysis==1.0.0"

from auckland_transport_analysis import generate_all_figures
figures = generate_all_figures('client_data/')


GIS-Specific Benefits
Standardise CRS Handling
# Every function handles CRS consistently
from auckland_gis import ensure_nztm

def calculate_area(gdf):
    gdf = ensure_nztm(gdf)  # Always EPSG:2193
    return gdf.geometry.area
Validate Spatial Joins
from auckland_gis import validate_join

# Catches when 5 SA2 zones silently disappear
result, report = validate_join(boundaries, census, key='SA2_code')
if not report['all_matched']:
    print(f"WARNING: {report['unmatched_count']} zones missing!")
Reusable Visualisations
from auckland_gis.viz import create_choropleth

# Same colour scale, same layout, every time
fig = create_choropleth(gdf, column='density', title='Population Density')


Python Package Terminology
Before we build, let’s clarify terms:
Module: A single Python file
# metrics.py is a module
def calculate_density(gdf):
    pass
Package: A directory of modules with __init__.py
auckland_gis/           # This is a package
├── __init__.py         # Makes it importable
├── data.py            # Module
├── metrics.py         # Module
└── viz.py             # Module
Distribution: The bundled, installable version
# These files on PyPI are distributions:
auckland_gis-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl  # Wheel (fast install)
auckland_gis-1.0.0.tar.gz            # Source distribution
Library vs Application: - Library: Imported by other code (geopandas, osmnx) - Application: Run directly (qgis, jupyter)
We’re building libraries in this course.

title: 4.1. Package Fundamentals: Structure, Configuration, and Building
text:
Part 2: Project Structure That Scales

The src/ Layout (Best Practice)
Modern Python packaging uses the src/ layout:
geohello/                      # Project root
├── src/                       # Source code here
│   └── geohello/             # Actual package
│       ├── __init__.py       # Makes it a package
│       └── core.py           # Your code
├── tests/                    # Tests separate from source
│   └── test_core.py
├── docs/                     # Documentation
├── pyproject.toml           # Package configuration
├── README.md                # Project description
└── LICENSE                  # Open source license
Why src/ instead of flat layout?
❌ Flat layout (old way):
geohello/
├── geohello/         # Package
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── core.py
├── tests/
└── pyproject.toml
Problems: - Tests might import from local directory instead of installed package - Hard to tell if tests pass because code works or because of accidental local imports
✅ src/ layout (modern way):
geohello/
├── src/
│   └── geohello/     # Package
├── tests/
└── pyproject.toml
Benefits: - Forces tests to use installed package - Catches import errors earlier - Clearer separation of concerns - Industry standard


Directory Structure Explained
Let’s build a real GIS package structure:
auckland-gis/                       # GitHub repo name (with hyphen)
├── src/
│   └── auckland_gis/              # Python package name (with underscore)
│       ├── __init__.py            # Package initialisation
│       ├── data.py                # Data loading functions
│       ├── metrics.py             # Calculation functions
│       └── viz.py                 # Visualisation functions
├── tests/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── test_data.py              # Test data loading
│   ├── test_metrics.py           # Test calculations
│   └── fixtures/                 # Test data files
│       └── sample_sa2.gpkg
├── docs/
│   ├── index.md                  # Documentation homepage
│   ├── quickstart.md
│   └── api-reference.md
├── examples/
│   └── basic_usage.ipynb         # Example notebook
├── pyproject.toml                # Package configuration
├── README.md                     # Project description
├── LICENSE                       # e.g., MIT License
└── .gitignore                    # Git ignore file


What Goes in __init__.py?
The __init__.py file makes a directory a Python package and controls what’s importable:
Minimal __init__.py (for starters):
"""Auckland GIS utilities for urban analytics."""

__version__ = "0.1.0"
Better __init__.py (export key functions):
"""Auckland GIS utilities for urban analytics."""

__version__ = "0.1.0"

from .data import load_sa2, load_pedestrian_counts
from .metrics import calculate_density, calculate_accessibility
from .viz import create_choropleth

__all__ = [
    "load_sa2",
    "load_pedestrian_counts",
    "calculate_density",
    "calculate_accessibility",
    "create_choropleth",
]
Now users can:
from auckland_gis import load_sa2  # Clean!
# Instead of:
from auckland_gis.data import load_sa2  # More verbose


Module Organisation Principles
1. Group by functionality, not type
❌ Don’t do this:
src/auckland_gis/
├── functions.py       # Too vague!
├── classes.py         # Too vague!
└── utilities.py       # Too vague!
✅ Do this:
src/auckland_gis/
├── data.py           # Data loading/validation
├── metrics.py        # Calculations
├── network.py        # Network analysis
└── viz.py            # Visualisation
2. Keep modules focused
Each module should have one clear purpose:
# data.py - Data loading and validation
def load_sa2(path=None): ...
def load_census(year=2023): ...
def validate_geometry(gdf): ...

# metrics.py - Calculations only
def calculate_density(gdf, pop_col='population'): ...
def calculate_accessibility(gdf, poi_gdf, max_distance_m=800): ...

# viz.py - Visualisation only
def create_choropleth(gdf, column, cmap='YlOrRd'): ...
def plot_network(G, node_color='red'): ...
3. Use subpackages for complex projects
For larger packages:
src/auckland_gis/
├── __init__.py
├── data/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── boundaries.py
│   └── census.py
├── analysis/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── spatial.py
│   └── temporal.py
└── viz/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── maps.py
    └── charts.py


Data in Packages: Best Practices
❌ Don’t ship large data files
# Bad: 50MB shapefile in the package
src/auckland_gis/
└── data/
    └── boundaries_large.shp  # Makes pip install slow!
✅ Do ship small reference data
# Good: Small lookup tables, schemas
src/auckland_gis/
└── data/
    └── sa2_schema.json    # 2KB - fine!
✅ Do provide download functions
# auckland_gis/data.py
def load_sa2(path=None):
    """
    Load Auckland SA2 boundaries.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    path : str, optional
        Path to local .gpkg file. If None, downloads from
        data repository.
    """
    if path is None:
        path = download_boundaries()  # Downloads on first use
    
    return gpd.read_file(path)
✅ Do use data repositories

Host large files on Zenodo, Figshare, or GitHub releases
Download on first use
Cache locally
